etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English smothe, smethe, from Old English smēþe, smōþ, both from Proto-West Germanic *smanþī, of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots smuith (“smooth”), Low German smood and smödig (“smooth, malleable, ductile”), Dutch smeuïg (“smooth”) (from earlier smeudig).

definitions.definition: Having a texture that lacks friction. Not rough.

quote.citation: 1695, C[harles] A[lphonse] du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica. The Art of Painting, […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Heptinstall for W. Rogers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The outlines must be smooth,  […] imperceptible to the touch, and even, without eminence or cavities.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter IX, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “A tight little craft,” was Austin’s invariable comment on the matron; and she looked it, always trim and trig and smooth of surface like a converted yacht cleared for action. ¶ Near her wandered her husband, orientally bland, invariably affable, […].

quote.citation: 2005, Lesley Brown, Sophist, translation of original by Plato, page 229e:
quote.text: Teaching that’s done by talking seems to have one rough path and another part which is smoother.

definitions.definition: Without difficulty, problems, or unexpected consequences or incidents.

quote.citation: 2011, Phil McNulty, “Euro 2012: Montenegro 2-2 England”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: England's path to Poland and Ukraine next summer looked to be a smooth one as goals from Ashley Young and Darren Bent gave them a comfortable lead after 31 minutes.

quote.citation: 2019 June 19, Elisabeth Malkin and Ana Swanson, “Mexico Ratifies Trade Deal With the U.S. and Canada”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: The path to approval has been bumpiest in Washington, where Democrats in Congress have raised concerns over Mexico’s enforcement of labor rights and environmental law — and smoothest in Mexico, where the president has described the accord as a guarantee of stability for his country’s economy.

definitions.definition: Bland; glib.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: This smooth discourse and mild behavior oft / Conceal a traitor.

quote.citation: 1912, Gustavus Myers, History of the Supreme Court of the United States, page 133:
quote.text: This feeling, grounded on the experience of centuries of oppression, was not to be allayed by smooth explanations on the part of the advocates of the Constitution.

definitions.definition: Flowing or uttered without check, obstruction, or hesitation; not harsh; fluent.

quote.citation: 1670, John Milton, The History of Britain:
quote.text: the only smooth poet of those times

quote.citation: 1737, [Alexander Pope], The First Epistle of the Second Book of Horace, Imitated, London:  […]  T. Cooper, […], →OCLC, page 16:
quote.text: VValler vvas ſmooth; but Dryden taught to join / The varying verſe, the full reſounding line, / The long majetſic march, and energy divine.

quote.citation: 1713 (indicated as 1714), [John] Gay, “Book III”, in The Fan. A Poem. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 23:
quote.text: VVhen bright Minerva roſe, / From her ſvveet Lips ſmooth Elocution flovvs,  […]

definitions.definition: Suave; sophisticated.

quote.citation: 2003, T. Lewis Humphrey, The Price of Love, →ISBN, page 279:
quote.text: He was so smooth and handsome. He knew just what to say and when to say it.

definitions.definition: (of an action) Natural; unconstrained.

quote.citation: 2006, Mary Kay Moskal, Camille Blachowicz, Reading for Fluency, →ISBN, page 3:
quote.text: In order for a reading to be smooth and effortless, readers must be able to recognize and read words accurately, automatically, and quickly.

definitions.definition: (of a motion) Unbroken.

quote.citation: 1927, United States National Guard Bureau, Manual of Basic Training and Standards of Proficiency for the National Guard, page 181:
quote.text: Demonstrate first by the numbers and then as one smooth movement.

definitions.definition: (chiefly of water) Placid, calm.

quote.citation: 1898, John Donaldson Ford, An American Cruiser in the East, page 47:
quote.text: As we worked to the southward, we picked up fair weather, and enjoyed smooth seas and pleasant skies.

definitions.definition: (of an edge) Lacking projections or indentations; not serrated.

quote.citation: 1994, Robert E. Swanson, A Field Guide to the Trees and Shrubs of the Southern Appalachians, →ISBN, page 8:
quote.text: A leaf having a smooth margin, without teeth or indentations of any kind, is called entire.

quote.citation: 1997, Christopher Dickey, Innocent Blood: A Novel, →ISBN, page 91:
quote.text: Out of the handles flipped the smooth blade and the serrated blade, which was dangerously sharp, the flathead screwdrivers, the Phillips screwdriver, the can opener, the awl.

definitions.definition: (of food or drink) Not grainy; having an even texture.

quote.citation: 1997, Lou Seibert Pappas, Sorbets and Ice Creams, →ISBN, page 19:
quote.text: A compact and stylish design, it produces 1 generous quart of excellent, smooth ice cream in 20 to 25 minutes.

definitions.definition: (of a beverage) Having a pleasantly rounded flavor; neither rough nor astringent.

quote.citation: 2002, Candace Irvin, For His Eyes Only, →ISBN, page 9:
quote.text: The coffee was smooth, so smooth she took another sip.

definitions.definition: (mathematics, of a function) Having derivatives of all finite orders at all points within the function’s domain.

quote.citation: 2003, Eric W. Weisstein, CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics, →ISBN, page 419:
quote.text: Any ANALYTIC FUNCTION is smooth. But a smooth function is not necessarily analytic.

definitions.definition: (mathematics, of a number) That factors completely into small prime numbers.
(linguistics, classical studies, of a vowel) Lacking marked aspiration.

quote.citation: 1830, Benjamin Franklin Fisk, A Grammar of the Greek Language, page 5:
quote.text: Οὐ becomes οὐκ before a smooth vowel, and οὐχ before an aspirate.

definitions.definition: (of muscles, medicine) Involuntary and non-striated.
Smoothly.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies. […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep.

definitions.definition: Something that is smooth, or that goes smoothly and easily.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis 27:16:
quote.text: The smooth of his neck.

quote.citation: 1861 January – 1862 August, W[illiam] M[akepeace] Thackeray, The Adventures of Philip on His Way through the World; […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London: Smith, Elder and Co., […], published 1862, →OCLC:
quote.text: I think you and I will take the ups and the downs , the roughs and the smooths of this daily existence and conversation

quote.citation: 1860, Anne Manning, The Day of Small Things‎[3], page 81:
quote.text: Things are often equalized by roughs and smooths being set against one another.

definitions.definition: A smoothing action.

quote.citation: 2006, Julienne Van Loon, Road Story‎[4], →ISBN, page 12:
quote.text: She brushes down her hair with a little bit of spit and a smooth of her hand and opens the bright green door, walking a few metres, squinting.

definitions.definition: A domestic animal having a smooth coat.

quote.citation: 1916, William Ernest Castle, Sewall Wright, Studies of Inheritance in Guinea-pigs and Rats‎[5], page 104:
quote.text: In the 4-toe stock there is a wide gap between the lowest rough and the smooths which come from the same parents.

definitions.definition: A member of an anti-hippie fashion movement in 1970s Britain.

quote.citation: 1999, Peter Childs, Mike Storry, Encyclopedia of Contemporary British Culture‎[6], →ISBN, page 188:
quote.text: By the early 1970s, skinhead culture began to mutate into the variant ‘white ethnic’ styles of the suedeheads and smooths.

definitions.definition: (statistics) The analysis obtained through a smoothing procedure.

quote.citation: 1990, Wolfgang Härdle, Applied Nonparametric Regression‎[7], →ISBN, page 17:
quote.text: A smooth of the potato data set has already been given in Figure 1.2.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make smooth or even.

quote.citation: 1961, William Gibson, The Miracle Worker‎[8], →ISBN, page 37:
quote.text: She smooths her skirt, looking as composed and ladylike as possible.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reduce to a particular shape or form by pressure; to press, to flatten.
(transitive) To make straightforward or easy.

quote.citation: 2007, Beth Kohn, Lonely Planet Venezuela, page 379:
quote.text: Caracas can be a tough place but the tremendously good-natured caraqueños smoothed my passage every step of the way.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To calm or palliate.
(statistics, image processing, digital audio) To capture important patterns in the data, while leaving out noise.

quote.citation: 1999, Murray R. Spiegel, Larry J. Stephens, Schaum’s Outline of Theory and Problems of Statistics‎[9], →ISBN, page 457:
quote.text: […]  the 7-month moving averages provide better smoothing of the data in this case than do the 3-month moving averages.

definitions.definition: (West Country) To stroke; especially to stroke an animal's fur.
